chapterTitle: Navigating the 3D Environment and Basic Object Manipulation
aiGenerationNote: Create a 15-minute live coding/demonstration video. Start by showing efficient camera navigation using WASD, right-click, scroll wheel, and the 'F' key. Then, demonstrate inserting various Part shapes (Block, Cylinder, Wedge). Systematically walk through the usage of the Select, Move, Scale, and Rotate tools, emphasizing the coordinate axes and common pitfalls like not selecting the correct tool. Dedicate a significant portion to modifying Part properties in the Properties window, specifically `Size`, `Position`, `Color`, `Material`, `Transparency`, and critically, `Anchored`. screens.title: Navigating the 3D Environment and Basic Object Manipulation
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you’ll become comfortable moving inside Roblox Studio, create and manipulate Parts, and learn the small set of tools and properties that let simple shapes become game-ready structures. Good camera navigation saves time: you’ll learn how to look, fly, zoom, and instantly focus on a selected object so you never lose your place. Parts are the fundamental building blocks: knowing their shapes and core properties helps you make walls, pillars, and props that behave predictably. You’ll practice the Select, Move, Scale and Rotate tools so you can place, size and orient objects precisely. We’ll also dive into the Properties window, focusing on Size, Position, Material, Color, Transparency and the critical Anchored flag that determines whether a part obeys physics. Finally you’ll group parts into Models to keep the Explorer tidy and move multi-part objects as a single unit. By the end of this chapter you will know how to avoid the most common beginner mistake — forgetting to anchor static parts — and you’ll have a short hands-on activity to practice these skills. Ready to build with confidence? Let’s start with efficient camera movement and how to keep your view aligned with your work.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you'll develop practical, verifiable skills. First, you will master camera navigation so you can inspect any scene quickly and return focus to selected parts. Second, you'll understand Parts: what they are and how the basic shapes are inserted into the workspace. Third through sixth, you'll learn the four transformation tools — Select, Move, Scale and Rotate — each with a clear use case and keyboard shortcut so you can manipulate objects precisely. Finally, you'll learn to read and modify essential properties such as Size, Position, Color, Material, Transparency, and Anchored, and you'll practice grouping parts into a Model to manage complex assemblies. Each objective is paired with a short verification step so you can confirm competency. These objectives matter because they turn clicks into a repeatable workflow: efficient navigation and consistent use of tools and properties let you iterate quickly and avoid common mistakes like unanchored parts falling during play tests. Practice the short activities, then test by running your scene and observing behavior.

screens.title: Camera Navigation — Move, Look, Zoom, and Focus
screens.narratorSegment: Efficient navigation in the Viewport is the foundation of fast building. The common control pattern mirrors first-person navigation: hold the right mouse button to look around and use the WASD keys to fly horizontally. W moves you forward, S back, A left and D right. Use the scroll wheel to zoom in and out for quick distance adjustments. For precise vertical movement, Q moves down and E moves up in many configurations. A powerful productivity shortcut is the F key, which focuses the camera on a selected object — the Viewport will center and zoom to that part so you can start editing immediately. Practice this by inserting a Block, selecting it, pressing F, then orbiting with right-click and flying with WASD until you can return to the block reliably. A common beginner mistake is panning with the wrong mouse button or expecting the scroll wheel to always change distance relative to the object's center. If you ever feel lost, select the part in the Explorer and press F to regain orientation. Why this matters: seamless camera control reduces time spent adjusting the view and lets you concentrate on composition and placement. Try the focus shortcut now and ask yourself: can I place a part precisely while keeping the camera centered on it?

keyIdea.title: Camera fluency
keyIdea.text: Master right-click look + WASD + scroll + Q/E and use F to instantly center on selected objects.

content.html:
Core Concept

Camera Navigation

Practice: insert a Part, select it, press F to focus, then use right-click plus WASD to fly around it. Use scroll wheel to adjust distance.

Step 1 — Look & Fly
Hold right-click to look; press W/A/S/D to move horizontally while looking in the direction you face.
Step 2 — Vertical & Zoom
Use Q and E for vertical adjustments and scroll wheel to zoom in and out smoothly.
Step 3 — Focus
Select a part in Explorer or Viewport and press F to center and zoom to it. This regains orientation instantly.
Key Takeaway

Camera shortcuts let you inspect geometry rapidly. Use F whenever you lose your place.

Visual: Navigation Callouts
Try it now
Insert a Part, press F, then orbit, fly, and zoom. Repeat until it feels natural.
Common Mistake
Panning without right-click or expecting scroll to always center on the object. Use F to regain focus.
Pro Tip
Select an object in Explorer and press F to instantly center it even if it's out of view.

screens.title: Parts — Fundamentals and Available Shapes
screens.narratorSegment: A Part in Roblox Studio is the basic 3D object you use to build geometry. Think of Parts as labeled blocks you place, size, color and materialize to form the world. The common Part shapes are Block (a cube or rectangular prism), Sphere, Cylinder, Wedge and CornerWedge. Each part is an independent object with its own Properties like Name, Position, Size and Orientation. When you insert a Part it appears at the center of the Viewport; good practice is to immediately give it a descriptive Name using the Explorer so you can find it later — for example, MainWall, FloorTile or Pillar. Naming is not cosmetic: it makes selection and focus faster as your scene grows. Concrete example: insert a Block, rename it FloorTile, scale it to a wide flat rectangle, change Material to Concrete and set Color to dark grey. By doing this you’ve created a reusable floor element. A common misconception is that a Part must be complicated to be useful; in truth, complex objects are usually collections of simple parts grouped into a Model. The takeaway: understand Part types and establish a naming habit now so your builds stay manageable.

keyIdea.title: Parts are objects
keyIdea.text: Parts are single objects with properties and a type (Block, Sphere, Cylinder, Wedge). Name them descriptively for easier management.

content.html:
Definition

Parts — the building blocks

Parts are the atomic 3D objects used to build every static and interactive element. Each part has properties that control appearance and behavior.

Common Shapes
Block, Sphere, Cylinder, Wedge and CornerWedge. Insert via the Model tab.
Naming Best Practice
Give parts descriptive names like FloorTile, MainWall or Pillar so you can find and focus them quickly with the Explorer.
Concrete Example
Insert a Block, rename it FloorTile, set Material to Concrete, color to dark grey, scale it wide and flat. This becomes a reusable floor element.
Visual: Part Types
Block
Default rectangular prism used for floors and walls.
Sphere
Smooth round object for decorative elements or indicators.
Cylinder
Good for pillars and rounded supports.
Wedge / CornerWedge
Use for ramps, slopes and trimmed corners.
Common Mistake
Assuming one complex Part replaces a group of simple parts. Complex shapes are usually groups of simple parts arranged together.

screens.title: Select Tool — How selection works and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Selection is the first step before any transform. The Select tool highlights chosen parts and draws a bounding box around them. You can select by clicking in the Viewport or by choosing parts in the Explorer. Using the Select tool reliably matters because transforms — Move, Scale and Rotate — act on whatever is selected; a wrong selection can move or resize the wrong object. Keyboard shortcuts help speed selection: Ctrl or Cmd + 1 activates the Select tool. When multiple parts are selected, the bounding box surrounds the combined selection and your transforms affect them together. A common beginner error is to assume the Explorer selection always matches what is visible; sometimes a small part hidden behind another remains selected. Verify your selection visually: the bounding box and gizmos will reveal the selection and available transformation handles. Concrete example: select a Block FloorTile in the Explorer, watch it center in the Viewport when you press F, then use Move so only the tile moves. Misconception check: grouping parts creates a Model, but selecting the Model in Explorer selects the whole group unless you drill down to individual children. Final takeaway: confirm what’s selected before transforming to avoid accidental edits.

content.html:
Definition

Select Tool

Select highlights parts and shows a bounding box and available gizmos. Use Explorer or Viewport clicks. Shortcut: Ctrl/Cmd + 1.

Visual Confirmation
The bounding box and gizmos tell you precisely which part(s) are selected. If it’s wrong, deselect and pick again.
Multiple Selection
Hold Ctrl/Cmd and click parts or drag a selection box to select many. Transforms affect the combined selection.
Common Mistake
Assuming Explorer selection is visible; hidden children may be selected. Use F to focus and confirm.
Example Workflow
Step A — Select via Explorer
Click a part name in Explorer, then press F. The Viewport will frame the part so you can verify selection visually.
Step B — Select in Viewport
Click directly on a part in the Viewport. Look for the bounding box, then confirm before moving or rotating.
Step C — Multi-select
Hold Ctrl/Cmd to pick multiple parts, or drag to draw a selection box around many parts, then group if needed.
Check Before Transforming
Look for gizmo arrows or rings — these appear only when selection is active and the correct tool is chosen.

screens.title: Move Tool — Move precisely along X, Y, Z axes
screens.narratorSegment: The Move tool repositions parts in 3D space. Activate it with Ctrl or Cmd + 2, then look for the three colored arrows: red for X (left-right), green for Y (up-down), and blue for Z (forward-backward). Drag a colored arrow to constrain motion strictly along that axis. Drag the central sphere to move freely on a plane defined by two axes. For example, to lift an object straight up, drag the green arrow; to slide it forward, drag the blue arrow. A practical scenario: you have a pillar and need to place a round Sphere on top of it. Select the Sphere, press Ctrl+2, drag the green arrow upward until the Sphere rests on the pillar's top surface. A common misconception is thinking the colored arrows represent colors only; they are the coordinate axes and correspond to the coordinate system visible in most scenes. Another mistake is dragging the wrong arrow because the camera angle foreshortens the gizmo; rotate the camera or use F to reframe before moving. When moving multiple objects, the center of the combined bounding box is used as the gizmo origin, so your movement may feel different than moving a single object. Final takeaway: use axis constraints for precision and confirm final placement by inspecting from multiple angles.

keyIdea.title: Axis-aware movement
keyIdea.text: Use colored gizmo arrows (red=X, green=Y, blue=Z) to constrain moves and the center sphere for planar translation.

content.html:
Process Flow

Move Tool

Constrain movement along an axis using colored arrows or move freely on a plane using the center handle. Shortcut: Ctrl/Cmd + 2.

Step 1 — Activate
Press Ctrl/Cmd + 2 to enable the Move gizmo when a part is selected.
Step 2 — Axis Moves
Drag red, green or blue arrows to move along X, Y, Z respectively. Use the center to drag on a plane.
Step 3 — Verify
Rotate the camera and confirm the part sits where intended from other angles. Use F to refocus if needed.
Check
If movement feels off with multi-selection, adjust individual parts or group them to standardize transforms.
Illustration: Axis Gizmo
Concrete Example
Place a Sphere on top of a Cylinder. Select the Sphere, activate Move, drag the green arrow up until it sits flush on the cylinder’s top surface.
Common Mistake
Dragging without checking axis orientation; camera foreshortening can make arrows hard to interpret. Reframe or press F to recenter.
Pro Tip
Use the Move center for planar adjustments and axis arrows for exact vertical or horizontal placement.

screens.title: Scale vs Rotate — How they change a Part
screens.narratorSegment: Scaling changes a part's Size dimensions, while rotating changes its Orientation. Scale alters width, height and depth values — you can scale uniformly to enlarge or shrink evenly or scale on a single axis to make a flat tile or a tall pillar. Rotation adjusts the Orientation angles around the X, Y and Z axes in degrees. Use Ctrl or Cmd + 3 for Scale and Ctrl or Cmd + 4 for Rotate. A clear example: to create a floor tile, scale a Block to be wide and shallow; to set its facing direction, rotate it by altering Orientation on the Y-axis. A frequent confusion is expecting Scale to change the pivot orientation; scaling does not reorient axes — rotation does. Another common error is accidentally scaling a grouped Model and expecting a single child to remain unchanged; grouped objects scale relative to the group's bounding box center. Concrete exercise: make a Block, scale it to 4x0.25x4 to become a tile, rotate it 45 degrees on Y to create a diagonal pattern. End with this check: did you change Size or Orientation, and does the object now fit visually and in coordinates where you want it?

keyIdea.title: Scale vs Rotate
keyIdea.text: Scale modifies Size; Rotate changes Orientation. Use axis controls and confirm results on multiple views.

content.html:
Comparison

Scale vs Rotate

Scale changes Size; Rotate changes Orientation. Both are necessary to position and shape parts correctly.

Scale (Ctrl/Cmd + 3)
Use spheres on faces and corners to adjust dimensions per axis or uniformly.
Rotate (Ctrl/Cmd + 4)
Use colored rings to spin parts around X, Y, Z; orientation values are measured in degrees.
Concrete Example
Scale a Block to 4 × 0.25 × 4 to form a floor tile, then rotate 45° on Y to lay it diagonally. Confirm placement from multiple camera angles.
Visuals & Tips
Misconception
Scaling does not change a part's orientation or pivot. Rotation changes facing but not size dimensions.
Group Effects
When scaling a grouped Model, children scale relative to the group's bounding box center. Ungroup to adjust individuals.
Pro Tip
Make small test adjustments and orbit the camera to check how scale and rotation interact visually with nearby parts.
Try This

Scale and rotate a Block to create a diagonal floor tile and verify that Size or Orientation changed as expected.

screens.title: Coordinate System — X, Y, Z and color coding
screens.narratorSegment: Roblox uses a right-handed 3D coordinate system with consistent color coding: red equals X (left-right), green equals Y (up-down), and blue equals Z (forward-backward). This color scheme is used throughout the Move, Scale and Rotate gizmos so when you see a green arrow you should immediately associate that with vertical movement. Understanding this mapping reduces errors when constraining transformations: for instance, if you want to raise a platform, use the green arrow to move it upward rather than dragging it on a plane. Another practical detail is orientation values are given as degrees per axis: Orientation lists rotation on X, Y and Z axes separately. A concrete scenario: you want to rotate a sign to face east. Determine which axis corresponds to yaw in your scene (usually Y), then rotate the sign by the required degrees on Y. A common misconception is assuming screen left-right equals X always — camera rotation changes screen directions, so rely on the gizmo colors rather than visual screen cues. Key practice: confirm axis color and test small adjustments, then check from another camera angle to ensure the part moved or rotated as intended. This habit keeps transforms predictable as scenes grow in complexity.

keyIdea.title: Axis color map
keyIdea.text: Red = X, Green = Y, Blue = Z. Use colors to orient moves and rotations reliably regardless of camera angle.

content.html:
Core Concept

Coordinate System

Red = X (left-right), Green = Y (up-down), Blue = Z (forward-backward). Gizmos use these colors to guide precise transforms.

Orientation Values
Orientation lists degrees rotated around X, Y, Z. Small angle changes often produce the desired visual effect.
Camera & Screen
Camera rotation changes screen directions; rely on gizmo color coding, not screen left-right, for accurate transforms.
Check Your Understanding
If you drag the blue arrow forward, has the part moved along depth relative to world coordinates? Confirm by reading Position values.
Axis Visual

screens.title: Properties Window — Key attributes and practical use
screens.narratorSegment: The Properties window is your control center for each Part’s attributes. Name helps you find parts in the Explorer. Position shows the exact X, Y, Z coordinates of the part’s center and is useful when you need reproducible placements. Size expresses width, height and depth so you can create consistent tiles and pillars. Orientation shows rotation in degrees around X, Y and Z. Color and Material affect visual appearance and how light interacts with the surface — choose Concrete for floors, Wood for pillars, Neon for bright UI-like elements. Transparency ranges from 0 for fully opaque to 1 for invisible. The Anchored property is critical: when true, the Part is fixed and will not be affected by gravity or collisions; when false, it participates in physics and can fall or be pushed. Practical example: create a floor tile, set Size to 4 × 0.25 × 4, set Material to Concrete and Anchored to true; this ensures the tile stays in place during tests. A frequent beginner mistake is leaving Anchored false for static structures so they collapse when running the game. Always check Anchored before Play. The Properties window also allows numeric entry for precise values — use it for repeatable placement across parts.

Practical example: create a floor tile, set Size to 4 × 0.25 × 4, set Material to Concrete and Anchored to true; this ensures the tile stays in place during tests. A frequent beginner mistake is leaving Anchored false for static structures so they collapse when running the game. Always check Anchored before Play. The Properties window also allows numeric entry for precise values — use it for repeatable placement across parts.

Definition

Properties Window

Edit attributes to control appearance and behavior. Numeric fields enable precise, repeatable values for size and position.

Name & Position
Name parts clearly; use Position to place objects precisely by X, Y, Z coordinates.
Size & Orientation
Size is width/height/depth; Orientation is rotation in degrees around each axis.
Visual & Physics
Color and Material affect look; Anchored toggles physics participation. Transparency controls visibility.
Practical Example
Create a Stable Floor Tile
Insert a Block, set Size to 4 × 0.25 × 4, Material to Concrete, Color to dark grey, Anchored to true. This prevents it from falling during Play.
Check Anchored
Before pressing Play, confirm Anchored=true for static structures; forgetting this causes collapses and wasted debugging time.
Numeric Precision
Enter exact Position and Size values in Properties to reuse placements across parts and scenes.
Key Takeaway

Properties let you control both what a part looks like and how it behaves. Anchored is crucial for static pieces.

screens.title: Anchored — Why it matters and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Anchored is one of the single most important Part properties for beginners. When Anchored is true the part is fixed in place and is unaffected by physics such as gravity or collisions. When Anchored is false the part participates in the physics simulation and can fall, tumble or be pushed by other objects. This distinction matters because most static game geometry — floors, walls, platforms — must be Anchored or they will collapse when you press Play. A concrete failure example: you build a multi-block tower and forget to anchor the blocks. On Play the tower falls through or topples because gravity affects each unanchored part. The fix is simple: select the parts, set Anchored to true in the Properties window, then Group them if you want to move them as a single unit. Another misconception is to anchor everything, including moving objects that need physics. For moving vehicles or physics-based props, Anchored should be false so the physics engine can operate. Final thought: check Anchored before testing; if a structure falls, that's the first property to verify. Ask yourself: should this object move during gameplay, or must it stay fixed?

content.html:
Core Concept

Anchored

Anchored = true fixes a part; Anchored = false allows physics to move it. This determines whether structures remain in place during Play.

Failure Example
A tower built of Blocks collapses during Play because Anchored=false. Fix: set Anchored=true for static pieces.
When Not to Anchor
Vehicles, physics toys and falling props should remain unanchored so the physics engine can move them naturally.
Pro Tip
If a structure falls, first inspect Anchored for all its parts before deep debugging. It often fixes the problem instantly.
Actionable Steps
Select All Parts
Hold Ctrl/Cmd and click each part or drag a selection box.
Set Anchored
In Properties, toggle Anchored to true for static pieces.
Group If Needed
Group parts into a Model to move them together; the group's composition retains each child's Anchored value.
Common Mistake

Anchoring everything prevents intended physics behaviors. Decide per-object whether it should be static or dynamic.

screens.title: Grouping & Models — Combine parts for easier management
screens.narratorSegment: Grouping lets you treat several Parts as a single unit. Select multiple parts by holding Ctrl or Cmd and clicking each one, or draw a selection box around them. Then press Ctrl+G / Cmd+G or use the Group button in the Model tab to create a Model in the Explorer that contains those parts. Models appear as a parent object; you can move, scale or rotate the entire Model together. If you need to edit an individual child, expand the Model in Explorer and select the child directly, or use Ungroup (Ctrl+U / Cmd+U) to separate them. A practical workflow: build a table from one tabletop Block and four Cylinder legs, group them into TableModel, then move the whole table while preserving the relative positions of the legs. Grouping keeps the Explorer tidy and reduces the chance of accidentally moving only one part. Beware: transforms applied to the group use the group's bounding box center as the origin, which can change how multi-part transforms behave compared to single part transforms. Final check: after grouping, test movement and then run Play to ensure Anchored settings are correct across all children.

Process Flow

Grouping & Models

Group parts to form Models that act as one object for transforms and Explorer organization.

Create a Group
Select parts, press Ctrl/Cmd + G or click Group in the Model tab. A Model node appears in Explorer.
Edit Children
Expand the Model in Explorer to select and edit individual parts, or Ungroup to separate them.
Group Caveat
Transforms on a group use the group's center; multi-part behavior may differ from per-part transforms. Check after grouping.
Concrete Example: Table Model
Step 1 — Build Parts
Create a Block for the tabletop and four Cylinder legs. Position legs at the corners of the tabletop.
Step 2 — Group
Select all five parts, press Ctrl/Cmd + G to make TableModel. Now move or rotate the table as a single unit.
Step 3 — Test
Run Play to ensure parts are Anchored if the table should remain static, or leave unanchored if it should respond to physics.
Key Takeaway

Grouping simplifies transforms and organization, but always verify Anchored and transforms after grouping.

screens.title: Activity: Build a Simple Anchored Structure
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity brings together the skills you've learned. Start a new Baseplate project if you don't have one open. Insert a Block, Cylinder and Sphere from the Model tab. Rename them FloorTile, Pillar and Orb in the Explorer to keep things clear. Select the Block, use Scale to make it wider and flatter — for example, 4 × 0.25 × 4 — set Material to Concrete and Color to dark grey, and set Anchored to true. Next, scale the Cylinder to a tall thin shape, move it atop the tile and change Material to Wood and Color to brown. Rotate it slightly for a natural look and set Anchored true. Scale the Sphere to a medium size, move it on top of the pillar, set Material to Neon, Color to bright yellow, and set Anchored true. Select all three parts and press Ctrl/Cmd + G to group into a Model and check that the Model appears in Explorer. Finally, press Play to test. If anything falls, stop and check Anchored on every part. This exercise verifies camera movement, selection, transform tools, property editing and grouping in one quick workflow. After testing, ask: did everything stay in place and is the Model manageable in Explorer?

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you’ll become comfortable moving inside Roblox Studio, create and manipulate Parts, and learn the small set of tools and properties that let simple shapes become game-ready structures. Good camera navigation saves time: you’ll learn how to look, fly, zoom, and instantly focus on a selected object so you never lose your place. Parts are the fundamental building blocks: knowing their shapes and core properties helps you make walls, pillars, and props that behave predictably. You’ll practice the Select, Move, Scale and Rotate tools so you can place, size and orient objects precisely. We’ll also dive into the Properties window, focusing on Size, Position, Material, Color, Transparency and the critical Anchored flag that determines whether a part obeys physics. Finally you’ll group parts into Models to keep the Explorer tidy and move multi-part objects as a single unit. By the end of this chapter you will know how to avoid the most common beginner mistake — forgetting to anchor static parts — and you’ll have a short hands-on activity to practice these skills. Ready to build with confidence? Let’s start with efficient camera movement and how to keep your view aligned with your work.

Over the next screens you'll develop practical, verifiable skills. First, you will master camera navigation so you can inspect any scene quickly and return focus to selected parts. Second, you'll understand Parts: what they are and how the basic shapes are inserted into the workspace. Third through sixth, you'll learn the four transformation tools — Select, Move, Scale and Rotate — each with a clear use case and keyboard shortcut so you can manipulate objects precisely. Finally, you'll learn to read and modify essential properties such as Size, Position, Color, Material, Transparency, and Anchored, and you'll practice grouping parts into a Model to manage complex assemblies. Each objective is paired with a short verification step so you can confirm competency. These objectives matter because they turn clicks into a repeatable workflow: efficient navigation and consistent use of tools and properties let you iterate quickly and avoid common mistakes like unanchored parts falling during play tests. Practice the short activities, then test by running your scene and observing behavior.

This second objectives slide expands the tools and the organizational habit set you’ll practice. You’ll learn each transform tool’s purpose and shortcut so you can work quickly: Select to pick parts, Move to reposition precisely along X, Y, and Z, Scale to resize by axis or uniformly, and Rotate to set orientation in degrees. We also make Properties an explicit objective: changing Size, Position, Color, Material and Transparency shapes appearance while Anchored controls physics behavior. Finally, grouping and ungrouping parts into a Model helps you treat collections as a single unit for transforms and organization. These processes are about repeatable habits: name parts clearly in Explorer, check which tool is active to avoid accidental transforms, and always verify Anchored settings before running the game. Each objective is paired with a small verification action so you can confirm competency while building your first anchored structure.

Efficient navigation in the Viewport is the foundation of fast building. The common control pattern mirrors first-person navigation: hold the right mouse button to look around and use the WASD keys to fly horizontally. W moves you forward, S back, A left and D right. Use the scroll wheel to zoom in and out for quick distance adjustments. For precise vertical movement, Q moves down and E moves up in many configurations. A powerful productivity shortcut is the F key, which focuses the camera on a selected object — the Viewport will center and zoom to that part so you can start editing immediately. Practice this by inserting a Block, selecting it, pressing F, then orbiting with right-click and flying with WASD until you can return to the block reliably. A common beginner mistake is panning with the wrong mouse button or expecting the scroll wheel to always change distance relative to the object's center. If you ever feel lost, select the part in the Explorer and press F to regain orientation. Why this matters: seamless camera control reduces time spent adjusting the view and lets you concentrate on composition and placement. Try the focus shortcut now and ask yourself: can I place a part precisely while keeping the camera centered on it?

A Part in Roblox Studio is the basic 3D object you use to build geometry. Think of Parts as labeled blocks you place, size, color and materialize to form the world. The common Part shapes are Block (a cube or rectangular prism), Sphere, Cylinder, Wedge and CornerWedge. Each part is an independent object with its own Properties like Name, Position, Size and Orientation. When you insert a Part it appears at the center of the Viewport; good practice is to immediately give it a descriptive Name using the Explorer so you can find it later — for example, MainWall, FloorTile or Pillar. Naming is not cosmetic: it makes selection and focus faster as your scene grows. Concrete example: insert a Block, rename it FloorTile, scale it to a wide flat rectangle, change Material to Concrete and set Color to dark grey. By doing this you’ve created a reusable floor element. A common misconception is that a Part must be complicated to be useful; in truth, complex objects are usually collections of simple parts grouped into a Model. The takeaway: understand Part types and establish a naming habit now so your builds stay manageable.

Selection is the first step before any transform. The Select tool highlights chosen parts and draws a bounding box around them. You can select by clicking in the Viewport or by choosing parts in the Explorer. Using the Select tool reliably matters because transforms — Move, Scale and Rotate — act on whatever is selected; a wrong selection can move or resize the wrong object. Keyboard shortcuts help speed selection: Ctrl or Cmd + 1 activates the Select tool. When multiple parts are selected, the bounding box surrounds the combined selection and your transforms affect them together. A common beginner error is to assume the Explorer selection always matches what is visible; sometimes a small part hidden behind another remains selected. Verify your selection visually: the bounding box and gizmos will reveal the selection and available transformation handles. Concrete example: select a Block FloorTile in the Explorer, watch it center in the Viewport when you press F, then use Move so only the tile moves. Misconception check: grouping parts creates a Model, but selecting the Model in Explorer selects the whole group unless you drill down to individual children. Final takeaway: confirm what’s selected before transforming to avoid accidental edits.

The Move tool repositions parts in 3D space. Activate it with Ctrl or Cmd + 2, then look for the three colored arrows: red for X (left-right), green for Y (up-down), and blue for Z (forward-backward). Drag a colored arrow to constrain motion strictly along that axis. Drag the central sphere to move freely on a plane defined by two axes. For example, to lift an object straight up, drag the green arrow; to slide it forward, drag the blue arrow. A practical scenario: you have a pillar and need to place a round Sphere on top of it. Select the Sphere, press Ctrl+2, drag the green arrow upward until the Sphere rests on the pillar's top surface. A common misconception is thinking the colored arrows represent colors only; they are the coordinate axes and correspond to the coordinate system visible in most scenes. Another mistake is dragging the wrong arrow because the camera angle foreshortens the gizmo; rotate the camera or use F to reframe before moving. When moving multiple objects, the center of the combined bounding box is used as the gizmo origin, so your movement may feel different than moving a single object. Final takeaway: use axis constraints for precision and confirm final placement by inspecting from multiple angles.

Scaling changes a part's Size dimensions, while rotating changes its Orientation. Scale alters width, height and depth values — you can scale uniformly to enlarge or shrink evenly or scale on a single axis to make a flat tile or a tall pillar. Rotation adjusts the Orientation angles around the X, Y and Z axes in degrees. Use Ctrl or Cmd + 3 for Scale and Ctrl or Cmd + 4 for Rotate. A clear example: to create a floor tile, scale a Block to be wide and shallow; to set its facing direction, rotate it by altering Orientation on the Y-axis. A frequent confusion is expecting Scale to change the pivot orientation; scaling does not reorient axes — rotation does. Another common error is accidentally scaling a grouped Model and expecting a single child to remain unchanged; grouped objects scale relative to the group's bounding box center. Concrete exercise: make a Block, scale it to 4x0.25x4 to become a tile, rotate it 45 degrees on Y to create a diagonal pattern. End with this check: did you change Size or Orientation, and does the object now fit visually and in coordinates where you want it?

Roblox uses a right-handed 3D coordinate system with consistent color coding: red equals X (left-right), green equals Y (up-down), and blue equals Z (forward-backward). This color scheme is used throughout the Move, Scale and Rotate gizmos so when you see a green arrow you should immediately associate that with vertical movement. Understanding this mapping reduces errors when constraining transformations: for instance, if you want to raise a platform, use the green arrow to move it upward rather than dragging it on a plane. Another practical detail is orientation values are given as degrees per axis: Orientation lists rotation on X, Y and Z axes separately. A concrete scenario: you want to rotate a sign to face east. Determine which axis corresponds to yaw in your scene (usually Y), then rotate the sign by the required degrees on Y. A common misconception is assuming screen left-right equals X always — camera rotation changes screen directions, so rely on the gizmo colors rather than visual screen cues. Key practice: confirm axis color and test small adjustments, then check from another camera angle to ensure the part moved or rotated as intended. This habit keeps transforms predictable as scenes grow in complexity.

The Properties window is your control center for each Part’s attributes. Name helps you find parts in the Explorer. Position shows the exact X, Y, Z coordinates of the part’s center and is useful when you need reproducible placements. Size expresses width, height and depth so you can create consistent tiles and pillars. Orientation shows rotation in degrees around X, Y and Z. Color and Material affect visual appearance and how light interacts with the surface — choose Concrete for floors, Wood for pillars, Neon for bright UI-like elements. Transparency ranges from 0 for fully opaque to 1 for invisible. The Anchored property is critical: when true, the Part is fixed and will not be affected by gravity or collisions; when false, it participates in physics and can fall or be pushed. Practical example: create a floor tile, set Size to 4 × 0.25 × 4, set Material to Concrete and Anchored to true; this ensures the tile stays in place during tests. A frequent beginner mistake is leaving Anchored false for static structures so they collapse when running the game. Always check Anchored before Play. The Properties window also allows numeric entry for precise values — use it for repeatable placement across parts.

Grouping lets you treat several Parts as a single unit. Select multiple parts by holding Ctrl or Cmd and clicking each one, or draw a selection box around them. Then press Ctrl+G / Cmd+G or use the Group button in the Model tab to create a Model in the Explorer that contains those parts. Grouping keeps the Explorer tidy and reduces the chance of accidentally moving only one part. Beware: transforms applied to the group use the group's bounding box center as the origin, which can change how multi-part transforms behave compared to single part transforms. Final check: after grouping, test movement and then run Play to ensure Anchored settings are correct across all children.

Rename them FloorTile, Pillar and Orb in the Explorer to keep things clear.
